items.caption:
Sublimation cannot print on 100% cotton. The chemistry doesn't work — the ink needs a polymer to bond into.

Any supplier telling you otherwise is going to coat the cotton, which changes the hand-feel, or deliver something that fades fast.

For a cotton range: screen print, embroidery, or heat transfer. Or change the fabric — a poly-cotton blend takes sublimation on the polyester fraction, softer and more muted. Sometimes that's the look you wanted anyway.

Pick the fabric for how the garment should feel, then pick decoration to suit. Doing it the other way round is how brands end up with a kit they don't like the feel of.

At 2 weeks you approve in April for a July delivery. At 14 weeks end to end, the same deadline means approving in January — committing to next season's kit before this season has finished.

The real cost of a long lead time isn't the waiting. It's deciding early, with worse information, and having no way to react when a club adds 200 pieces in May.

items.caption:
Three signs you're talking to a middleman rather than a manufacturer:

1. They can't show you this week's floor on a live video call. Anyone with a factory can — it takes 90 seconds.
2. Every photo shows the same corner of the same room. Real floors look different on different days.
3. They quote every product category. Nobody makes jerseys, shoes and backpacks in one building.

None of this makes a trading company a bad partner. But you should know which you're buying from, because it changes who controls your lead time.

Ask for a live walkthrough. We'll do one this week.

#sourcing #cutandsew #clothingbrandowner #clothingmanfacturer #manufacturing #teamwear

An embroidered crest, close up.

Multiple needles, one colour each, the machine swapping between them as the design builds. Thread sits on top of the fabric, which is why it feels the way it does and why it adds weight.

Best for crests and sponsor marks. Not for full-garment graphics — that's what sublimation is for.

#embroidery #satisfying #cutandsew #teamwear #clothingmanfacturer #howitsmade

If I were buying teamwear instead of making it, here's what I'd ask.

1. Which operations happen in this building, and which leave it? The answer tells you who controls your lead time.
2. Show me the floor, live, this week.
3. MOQ per colourway — not per style. That's where quotes go wrong.

5. What was the last order you got wrong? Every factory has one. How they answer tells you how they'll behave when it's yours.

Buyers under-ask 1 and 5 and over-weight price.

Sublimation press, 60 seconds at 200°C.

Blank polyester goes in with a paper transfer. The ink turns to gas, bonds inside the fibre, and the paper comes off grey.

Full-garment graphics, no hand-feel, nothing to peel.

The trade-off: polyester only, and it can't print white onto a dark base. Those are real limits, not fine print.

items.caption:
Four ways to decorate a kit, and the honest trade-offs.

SUBLIMATION — ink becomes part of the fabric. Zero hand-feel, nothing to peel, unlimited colour. Polyester only, and it can't print white onto dark.

EMBROIDERY — thread stitched in. The most premium feel, best for crests. Adds weight and cost.

HEAT TRANSFER — applied film. 3D, reflective, fluor, matt and silicone. Works on any fabric; application is everything.

SCREEN PRINT — ink on the surface. Cheapest at volume, one screen per colour.

The real answer is usually a mix. All four run in our building, so a garment using three of them doesn't leave and doesn't add a week.

#sublimation #embroidery #teamwear #footballkit #customkits #cutandsew

Names and numbers are where kit becomes a specific player's shirt, and where most complaints come from. Film that lifts at the corner after a season. Numbers that crack. Letters that bleed.

It comes down to four variables: the film, the temperature, the dwell time and the pressure. Get one wrong and it shows up three months later.

We run 3D, reflective, fluor, matt and silicone. The choice is usually about hand-feel and how far away it needs to read.

#teamwear #footballkit #heattransfer #customkits #nameset #apparelmanufacturing

Egypt signed the PEM Convention — the pan-Euro-Mediterranean rules of origin — on 9 October 2013, and the revised version of those rules has applied between the EU and Egypt since March 2025.

PEM allows diagonal cumulation. In plain terms: materials from another country in the zone can count towards local content. The zone covers the EU, EFTA, Türkiye, the Western Balkans and the Mediterranean partners.

So a garment cut and sewn in Egypt from Italian fabric can still qualify as Egyptian origin and enter the EU duty-free.

Two caveats, because origin rules punish the careless. Processing requirements vary by category. And the paperwork has changed — the EUR-MED certificate is gone, and since January 2026 only the revised rules apply. If you last looked at this before 2025, look again.

Confirm your category with your customs broker before building a cost model on it.

items.caption:
GSM = grams per square metre. It's fabric weight, and it's the number that matters most.

130–150 — match jersey. Light, fast-drying.
150–180 — training top. The everyday workhorse.
180–220 — polo, warm-up.
240–320 — hoodie, sweat.

Lighter isn't cheaper by accident — it's less yarn. If a factory quotes you without a GSM, you don't know what you're buying.

Ask for GSM and seam type before you ask for a price.

#fabric #gsm #teamwear #cutandsew #clothingmanufacturer #footballkit

A finished kit, and the decisions inside it.

Fabric: poly interlock, mid-weight, for stability and print quality.
Seams: flatlock at the shoulders and sides.
Body graphic: sublimated — printed before the panels were cut, so it runs edge to edge with no break.
Crest: embroidered.
Numbers: heat transfer, matt film.
Collar and cuffs: ribbed, with recovery that holds.
Label: heat transfer, nothing to itch.

None of these are default settings. Every one was chosen, and every one has a cheaper and a more expensive version.

That's what a tech pack conversation actually is.

items.caption:
Nine fabric words that appear on every teamwear quote.

INTERLOCK — double-knit, smooth both sides, more stable. Classic jersey body.
SINGLE JERSEY — lighter, one smooth face, curls at a raw edge.
PIQUÉ — textured waffle. The polo fabric.
MESH — open structure for airflow.
JACQUARD — pattern knitted into the fabric, not printed on.
MOISTURE WICKING — ask whether it's a finish or the fibre. A finish washes out.
SPANDEX — stretch content, 5–10% in a fitted kit.
RECOVERY — whether it returns to shape after stretching.

Recovery is the one brands skip, and it's why some kit looks baggy at the knees by March.

#fabric #teamwear #cutandsew #apparelmanufacturing #kitdesign #footballkit #textiles

A goalkeeper shirt isn't an outfield shirt with longer sleeves.

Elbow padding changes the sleeve construction. The fabric is heavier because it meets the ground repeatedly. The body is cut looser for reach. And the colour has to contrast with both teams and both other keepers, which is a rule, not a preference.

If your kit supplier quotes a keeper shirt at the same price as an outfield one, they haven't read the brief.

The thing that makes reorders work isn't speed alone — it's whether your supplier held the fabric lot. Ask about that before the season starts, not during it.

items.caption:
White kit goes grey for three reasons, and only one of them is the factory's fault.

1. Polyester picks up dye from other garments in the wash. Not fixable in manufacturing.
2. Optical brighteners wash out. They were never permanent.
3. Low-grade fabric with uneven whiteness to begin with. That one IS on the factory.

Ask for the whiteness grade on white polyester. It's a spec, and it's rarely volunteered.

items.caption:
Everyone tests stretch. Almost nobody tests recovery.

Stretch is how far the fabric goes. Recovery is whether it comes back.

Pull a cuff and let go. If it returns instantly, good recovery. If it stays slightly open, that's the shirt that'll look tired by March.

It's a two-second test and it tells you more than the composition label does.

Garments shrink because knit fabric relaxes in the first wash. That's physics, not a defect.

What separates a good supplier from a bad one is whether anyone measured it before cutting 2,000 pieces. A shrinkage test tells you the number, and the pattern gets graded to compensate.

Put a tolerance in your tech pack. ±3% is normal. ±5% means somebody skipped the test.

Most quality problems in teamwear aren't sewing problems. They're fabric problems nobody checked at intake, and they only surface after 2,000 garments are cut.

We inspect at 5 points: fabric arrival, pattern, bulk cut, special sewing, finishing.

The first one saves the most. Shade variance caught on an incoming roll costs a roll. Caught after cutting, it costs the order.

None of this is unusual. What's unusual is publishing it, so you can ask about a specific stage instead of asking "do you do QC?" — which every factory answers yes to.

Ask which stage catches shade variance, and who signs it off.

It's one of our five inspection points: piece count and placement checked against the marker before anything reaches a sewing line.

Four ways to decorate a kit, and the honest trade-offs.

SUBLIMATION — ink becomes part of the fabric. Zero hand-feel, nothing to peel, unlimited colour. Polyester only, and it can't print white onto dark.

EMBROIDERY — thread stitched in. The most premium feel, best for crests. Adds weight and cost.

HEAT TRANSFER — applied film. 3D, reflective, fluor, matt and silicone. Works on any fabric; application is everything.

SCREEN PRINT — ink on the surface. Cheapest at volume, one screen per colour.

The real answer is usually a mix. All four run in our building, so a garment using three of them doesn't leave and doesn't add a week.

GSM = grams per square metre. It's fabric weight, and it's the number that matters most.

130–150 — match jersey. Light, fast-drying.
150–180 — training top. The everyday workhorse.
180–220 — polo, warm-up.
240–320 — hoodie, sweat.

Lighter isn't cheaper by accident — it's less yarn. If a factory quotes you without a GSM, you don't know what you're buying.

Nine fabric words that appear on every teamwear quote.

INTERLOCK — double-knit, smooth both sides, more stable. Classic jersey body.
SINGLE JERSEY — lighter, one smooth face, curls at a raw edge.
PIQUÉ — textured waffle. The polo fabric.
MESH — open structure for airflow.
JACQUARD — pattern knitted into the fabric, not printed on.
MOISTURE WICKING — ask whether it's a finish or the fibre. A finish washes out.
SPANDEX — stretch content, 5–10% in a fitted kit.
RECOVERY — whether it returns to shape after stretching.

Recovery is the one brands skip, and it's why some kit looks baggy at the knees by March.

Sublimation cannot print on 100% cotton. The chemistry doesn't work — the ink needs a polymer to bond into.

Egyptian garment exports to Europe grew 46% in the first seven months of 2026, to $930m. Spain alone was up 86%.

There's a structural reason most brands sourcing in Asia don't know about.

1. The EU–Egypt Association Agreement has been in force since June 2004. Egyptian industrial goods — garments included — enter the EU without duty.
2. Egypt is in the pan-Euro-Mediterranean origin zone, so Turkish or European fabric can still count towards Egyptian origin.

If your fabric spec is European and you assumed that forced you into European manufacturing prices, it doesn't.

Figures: Egypt's Ready-Made Garments Export Council, September 2026. Confirm your own HS code with your customs broker — origin rules changed in 2025 and I'd rather you checked.

Egypt signed the PEM Convention — the pan-Euro-Mediterranean rules of origin — on 9 October 2013, and the revised version of those rules has applied between the EU and Egypt since March 2025.

PEM allows diagonal cumulation. In plain terms: materials from another country in the zone can count towards local content. The zone covers the EU, EFTA, Türkiye, the Western Balkans and the Mediterranean partners.

So a garment cut and sewn in Egypt from Italian fabric can still qualify as Egyptian origin and enter the EU duty-free.

Two caveats, because origin rules punish the careless. Processing requirements vary by category. And the paperwork has changed — the EUR-MED certificate is gone, and since January 2026 only the revised rules apply. If you last looked at this before 2025, look again.

Confirm your category with your customs broker before building a cost model on it.
